overview: Aardonyx celestae was a sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived in what is now South Africa during the Early Jurassic, approximately 201–193 million years ago. It reached an estimated length of over 8 metres and a mass of around 1,500 kilograms, making it one of the larger animals of its time and place. Fossils were recovered from the Elliot Formation of the Free State Province. Uniquely, the known remains represent two juvenile individuals, meaning the adults may have been even larger.

Aardonyx is scientifically significant as a transitional form between bipedal prosauropod ancestors and the fully quadrupedal sauropods that followed. Osteological evidence suggests it habitually walked on its hind legs but was anatomically capable of bearing weight on all four limbs. Named in 2009 by Yates and colleagues, it occupies a position within Sauropodiformes and illuminates the evolutionary pathway leading to the great long-necked giants of the Jurassic.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Aardonyx celestae was described in 2009 by Yates, Bonnan, Neveling, Chinsamy, and Blackbeard. The generic name derives from Afrikaans aard (earth) and Greek onyx (claw), meaning 'earth claw'. The species name honours Celeste Yates. The fossils were collected from excavations in the Free State Province of South Africa and represent only two individuals, both estimated to be under ten years old at the time of death.

articles.title: Anatomy and Locomotion
articles.body: Analysis of the limb bones indicates Aardonyx was primarily bipedal but could adopt a quadrupedal stance, making it a key transitional taxon. The radius and ulna show features consistent with occasional weight-bearing on the forelimbs. Bone histology confirmed the two specimens were still growing, suggesting adult individuals would have been substantially larger than the approximately 7-metre juveniles recovered.

articles.title: Ecology and Diet
articles.body: Aardonyx was a herbivore that fed on leaves and foliage from shrubs and trees. Its teeth were leaf-shaped with a sharp point suited to stripping vegetation from branches. The diet and feeding posture are interpreted as intermediate between its bipedal prosauropod ancestors and the high-browsing, quadrupedal sauropods that evolved later in the Jurassic.

articles.title: Palaeoenvironment
articles.body: The Elliot Formation in which Aardonyx was found represents a semi-arid to seasonally arid floodplain environment of the Early Jurassic. The formation has yielded numerous other early sauropodomorphs and small theropods, reflecting a diverse dinosaurian fauna that inhabited southern Gondwana during the opening stages of the Jurassic Period.

record.locomotion: Habitually bipedal; capable of quadrupedal walking
record.description: Aardonyx was a large early sauropodomorph from Early Jurassic South Africa. Its jaws and limbs preserve a combination of features associated with mostly bipedal ancestors and the bulk-feeding, quadrupedal sauropods that evolved later.
facts: The holotype BP/1/6254 is the rostral half of a left maxilla.
A nearby caudal left-maxilla fragment, BP/1/6505, may be part of the same bone as the holotype.

Referred material from Marc’s Quarry includes cranial and mandibular elements, cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal vertebrae, ribs, gastralia, chevrons, girdle elements, and bones of the forelimbs, hindlimbs, hands and feet.
The quarry assemblage appears to represent two immature individuals; the smaller individual is about 85 per cent of the larger in linear postcranial dimensions.
Histology of a rib and scapular fragment showed continuing growth and suggested that the sampled individual or individuals may have been younger than ten years at death.
The disarticulated material supports a broad anatomical reconstruction, but specimen association, adult proportions and soft tissues remain uncertain.

animalParagraphs: Aardonyx was a long-necked, small-headed plant-eater from what is now South Africa. The two known animals were about seven metres long when they died, but bone tissue shows that both were still growing, so the proportions and maximum size of a mature animal are not directly known.

Its jaws retain the narrow, pointed outline seen in earlier sauropodomorphs, while other features suggest a wider gape and a shift towards taking in vegetation in bulk. The particular plants it ate are not preserved.

The hindlimbs indicate habitual bipedal movement, but the forelimbs and feet also show features connected with bearing weight on all four limbs. This mosaic of traits makes Aardonyx useful for studying a gradual evolutionary transition rather than a simple halfway form.
animalHighlights: A long neck, small head and deep body placed Aardonyx within the early radiation of large-bodied sauropodomorphs.
Jaw anatomy combines a narrow snout with features associated with a wider gape and less selective bulk feeding.
Limb anatomy supports mostly two-legged movement while showing an increasing capacity for four-legged weight-bearing.

questions.title: How large was an adult?
questions.copy: Both known individuals were still growing. Larger adult estimates are extrapolations rather than measurements from a mature skeleton.

questions.title: Which bones belonged together?
questions.copy: The quarry material is disarticulated. The assemblage supports two individuals, but every bone cannot be assigned to a single associated skeleton.

questions.title: Exactly where does it sit on the family tree?
questions.copy: Analyses consistently place Aardonyx near the sauropod transition, but its precise relationship to other early sauropodomorphs varies.

review.ageReviewNote: The profile follows the Early Jurassic upper Elliot Formation assignment of the Marc’s Quarry type assemblage. The original description did not provide a narrow numerical radiometric age for the quarry.

evidence.summary: Numerous disarticulated bones from one quarry collectively represent most major skeletal regions of two immature individuals, but there is no complete, articulated or adult skeleton.
evidence.material: Holotype BP/1/6254, the rostral half of a left maxilla, plus disarticulated cranial, axial, girdle and limb material from Marc’s Quarry attributed to two immature individuals.

panel.headline: Partial skull and skeleton remains from two young animals.
panel.standfirst: Aardonyx is known from disarticulated skull, vertebral, girdle and limb bones representing at least two immature individuals. The name-bearing fossil is part of the upper jaw rather than a complete skeleton.

coverage.label: Moderate
coverage.basis: Most major skeletal regions are represented across the quarry assemblage, but the bones are disarticulated and neither individual is complete.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Collectively, the quarry material represents most major parts of the skeleton, including parts of the skull and jaws, vertebral column, shoulder and hip girdles, and all four limbs.
knownRemains.note: Because the bones were found disarticulated and both animals were still growing, the precise proportions and maximum adult size of Aardonyx remain uncertain.
